subjective.question: Why does measurement on the real line need the abstract theory of measure? Explain with reference to the length of an interval and the points in it.
subjective.answer: Length in R, area in R² and volume in R³ are concrete ways of measuring the 'size' of a set, and measure is the abstract concept that generalizes all of them. A single point on the real line has width (length) 0, so a point is negligible. The interval (0, 1] satisfies (0, 1] = (0, 1) ∪ {1}, and accordingly 1 = 1 + 0: the point contributes nothing. But (0, 1) is the union of its points, and it is an uncountable union; writing |(0, 1)| = sum of the lengths of its points would give 1 = 0 + 0 + 0 + …, which is meaningless. Hence 'the whole is the sum of its parts' (additivity) can only be demanded for countable disjoint decompositions, and a rigorous abstract theory — measure theory — is needed to handle infinity and the infinitesimal consistently.

subjective.question: State the three basic properties of length on R illustrated in the notes, with one example of each.
subjective.answer: (i) Monotonicity: if A ⊆ B then |A| ≤ |B|. For example (0, 1), (0, 1] and [0, 1) are subsets of [0, 1], so their lengths do not exceed |[0, 1]| = 1. (ii) Translation invariance: translating an interval does not change its length. For example [−1/2, 1/2] is [0, 1] shifted 1/2 unit to the left, and both have length 1. (iii) Additivity: the measure of a disjoint union is the sum of the measures. For example (0, 2] = (0, 1] ∪ (1, 2] gives |(0, 2]| = |(0, 1]| + |(1, 2]|, i.e. 2 = 1 + 1; and (0, 1] = (0, 1) ∪ {1} gives 1 = 1 + 0.

subjective.question: Define a ring of sets. Show that for X = {a, b, c}, the collection 䧀= {∅, X, {b}, {a, c}} is a ring.
subjective.answer: Definition: Let X ≠ ∅ and 䧀be a collection of subsets of X. Then 䧀is called a ring if for all A, B ∈ 䧀: (i) A ∪ B ∈ 䧀, and (ii) A − B ∈ 䧀. Verification: The only non-trivial pairs are formed from {b} and {a, c} together with ∅ and X. We have {b} ∪ {a, c} = X ∈ 䧀, {b} − {a, c} = {b} ∈ 䧀, {a, c} − {b} = {a, c} ∈ 䧀, X − {b} = {a, c} ∈ 䧀, {b} − X = ∅ ∈ 䧀, X − {a, c} = {b} ∈ 䧀, and unions/differences involving ∅ or equal sets give ∅, X or the set itself, all in 䧀. Hence both conditions hold for all A, B ∈ 䧀, so 䧀is a ring.

subjective.question: Prove that if 䧀is a ring of subsets of X, then (i) ∅ ∈ 䧀, (ii) A Δ B ∈ 䧀, and (iii) A ∩ B ∈ 䧀for all A, B ∈ 䧀.
subjective.answer: (i) For any A ∈ 䧀, the ring is closed under set difference, so A − A ∈ 䧀. But A − A = ∅, hence ∅ ∈ 䧀. (ii) For A, B ∈ 䧀we have A − B ∈ 䧀and B − A ∈ 䧀. Since a ring is closed under unions, A Δ B = (A − B) ∪ (B − A) ∈ 䧀. (iii) Write A ∪ B = [(A − B) ∪ (B − A)] ∪ (A ∩ B) = (A Δ B) ∪ (A ∩ B), where the union is disjoint. Hence A ∩ B = (A ∪ B) − (A Δ B). By (ii), A Δ B ∈ 䧀, and A ∪ B ∈ 䧀by the definition of a ring, so their difference A ∩ B ∈ 䧀.

subjective.question: Show that the collection 䧀of all finite subsets of N is a ring.
subjective.answer: Let A, B ∈ 䧀, so |A| < ∞ and |B| < ∞. Then A ∪ B is finite (a union of two finite sets is finite), so A ∪ B ∈ 䧀. Also A − B ⊆ A, and a subset of a finite set is finite, so A − B ∈ 䧀. Both ring conditions hold, hence 䧀is a ring.

subjective.question: Define a σ-ring and prove that every σ-ring is a ring.
subjective.answer: Definition: A collection 䧀of subsets of X ≠ ∅ is a σ-ring if (i) A − B ∈ 䧀for all A, B ∈ 䧀, and (ii) ∪ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ ∈ 䧀for every sequence {Aᵢ} of sets in 䧀. Proof: Let A, B ∈ 䧀. By (i), A − B ∈ 䧀. For the union, write A ∪ B = A ∪ B ∪ ∅ ∪ ∅ ∪ … as a countable union of members of 䧀(note ∅ = A − A ∈ 䧀by (i)). By (ii) this countable union belongs to 䧀, so A ∪ B ∈ 䧀. Thus 䧀satisfies both conditions of a ring, so every σ-ring is a ring.

subjective.question: Show that the ring of all finite subsets of N is not a σ-ring. Conclude that a ring need not be a σ-ring.
subjective.answer: Let 䧀= {A ⊆ N : |A| < ∞}, which is a ring. Consider the singletons {1}, {2}, {3}, …, each of which belongs to 䧀. Their countable union is ∪ᵢ₌₁^∞ {i} = N, and N is not finite, so N ∉ 䧀. Hence 䧀is not closed under countable unions and is therefore not a σ-ring. This example shows that a ring need not be a σ-ring (whereas every σ-ring is a ring).

subjective.question: Define a Boolean algebra (algebra of sets). Verify that for X = {a, b, c}, the collection 䧀= {∅, X, {a}, {b, c}} is a Boolean algebra.
subjective.answer: Definition: A collection 䧀of subsets of X ≠ ∅ is a Boolean algebra if (i) A ∪ B ∈ 䧀for all A, B ∈ 䧀, and (ii) A′ ∈䧀for all A ∈ 䧀. Verification: Complements: ∅′ = X ∈ 䧀, X′ = ∅ ∈ 䧀, {a}′ = {b, c} ∈ 䧀and ({b, c})′ = {a} ∈ 䧀, so condition (ii) holds. Unions: {a} ∪ {b, c} = X ∈ 䧀, and every union involving ∅, X or a set with itself is again a member of 䧀, so condition (i) holds. Hence 䧀is a Boolean algebra.

subjective.question: Prove that every algebra is a ring.
subjective.answer: Let 䧀be an algebra on X, so 䧀is closed under finite unions and complementation. Let A, B ∈ 䧀. We show A − B ∈ 䧀. Since A − B = A ∩ B′, it suffices to show A ∩ B′ ∈ 䧀. Now A′ ∈ 䧀by complementation, and B ∈ 䧀, so A′ ∪ B ∈ 䧀by closure under finite unions. Complementing again, (A′ ∪ B)′ ∈ 䧀. By De Morgan's law, (A′ ∪ B)′ = (A′)′ ∩ B′ = A ∩ B′. Hence A − B = A ∩ B′ ∈ 䧀. Also A ∪ B ∈ 䧀by the definition of an algebra. Therefore 䧀satisfies both ring conditions, so every algebra is a ring.

subjective.question: Prove that a ring 䧀of subsets of X is an algebra if and only if X ∈ 䧀.
subjective.answer: (⇒) Suppose the ring 䧀is an algebra. Since 䧀is a ring, for any A ∈ 䧀we have A − A = ∅ ∈ 䧀. Since 䧀is an algebra, it is closed under complementation, so ∅′ ∈ 䧀. But ∅′ = X, hence X ∈ 䧀. (⇐) Suppose X ∈ 䧀. For any A ∈ 䧀, A′ = X − A ∈ 䧀because a ring is closed under set difference; so 䧀is closed under complementation. A ring is already closed under finite unions. Hence 䧀satisfies both conditions of an algebra, so 䧀is an algebra.

subjective.question: Define a σ-algebra. Prove that a σ-algebra is closed under countable intersections and under set difference.
subjective.answer: Definition: A collection 䧀of subsets of X ≠ ∅ is a σ-algebra if (i) A′ ∈ 䧀for every A ∈ 䧀, and (ii) ∪ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ ∈ 䧀for every sequence {Aᵢ} of sets in 䧀. Countable intersections: Let {Aₙ} ⊆ 䧀. Each Aₙ′ ∈ 䧀by (i), so ∪ₙ Aₙ′ ∈ 䧀by (ii), and complementing again and using De Morgan's law, ∩ₙ Aₙ = (∪ₙ Aₙ′)′ ∈ 䧀. Set difference: For A, B ∈ 䧀, A − B = A ∩ B′. Now B′ ∈ 䧀by (i), and a finite intersection is a special case of a countable intersection, so A ∩ B′ ∈ 䧀. Hence A − B ∈ 䧀.

subjective.question: Show that 䧀= {A ⊆ N : A is countable or A′ is countable} is a σ-algebra on N, but the analogous class of subsets of R that are countable with countable complement is not a σ-algebra on R.
subjective.answer: On N: every subset of N is countable, and the complement of a subset of N is again a subset of N, hence countable. So on N the class of countable sets with countable complement is all of P(N), a σ-algebra; equivalently {A ⊆ N : A countable or A′ countable} = P(N). On R: consider Z ⊆ R. The set Z is countable, but its complement Z′ = R − Z is uncountable, so Z does not meet the 'countable with countable complement' requirement that the analogous class would demand. In fact the requirement is impossible on R: if A and A′ were both countable, then R = A ∪ A′ would be countable, a contradiction. So the N-construction collapses on R and the class is not a σ-algebra on R. The contrast comes from N being countable while R is uncountable.

subjective.question: Prove that a σ-ring is a σ-algebra if and only if it contains X.
subjective.answer: (⇒) If the σ-ring 䧀is a σ-algebra, then being an algebra it contains X: indeed for A ∈ 䧀, ∅ = A − A ∈ 䧀and complementation (available since 䧀is an algebra) gives X = ∅′ ∈ 䧀. (⇐) Suppose the σ-ring 䧀contains X. For A ∈ 䧀, A′ = X − A ∈ 䧀because a σ-ring is closed under set difference; so 䧀is closed under complementation. A σ-ring is already closed under countable unions. Hence 䧀satisfies both σ-algebra conditions, so 䧀is a σ-algebra.

subjective.question: Prove that an arbitrary intersection of σ-algebras on X is also a σ-algebra.
subjective.answer: Let 䫀= { 䧀_α : α ∈ I} be a family of σ-algebras on X ≠ ∅ and put 䧀= ∩_{α∈I} 䧀_α. We verify the two σ-algebra conditions. (i) Complements: Let A ∈ 䧀. Then A ∈ 䧀_α for every α ∈ I. Each 䧀_α is a σ-algebra, so A′ ∈ 䧀_α for every α, hence A′ ∈ ∩_{α∈I} 䧀_α = 䧀. (ii) Countable unions: Let {Aᵢ}ᵢ₌₁^∞ ⊆ 䧀. Then {Aᵢ} ⊆ 䧀_α for every α, so ∪ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ ∈ 䧀_α for every α since each 䧀_α is a σ-algebra. Hence ∪ᵢ₌₁^∞ Aᵢ ∈ ∩_{α∈I} 䧀_α = 䧀. By (i) and (ii),䧀is a σ-algebra.

subjective.question: Give a counter-example to show that the union of two σ-algebras need not be a σ-algebra.
subjective.answer: Let X = {a, b, c} and take 䧀₁ = {∅, X, {b}, {a, c}} and 䧀₂ = {∅, X, {c}, {a, b}}, which are both σ-algebras on X. Their union is 䧀₁ ∪ 䧀₂ = {∅, X, {b}, {c}, {a, c}, {a, b}}. Now {b} ∈ 䧀₁ ∪ 䧀₂ and {c} ∈ 䧀₁ ∪ 䧀₂, but {b} ∪ {c} = {b, c} ∉ 䧀₁ ∪ 䧀₂. So 䧀₁ ∪ 䧀₂ is not closed under (finite, hence countable) unions and is therefore not a σ-algebra.

subjective.question: Define the σ-algebra generated by a family ℬ of subsets of X. Find the σ-algebra generated by a single set A ⊆ X and justify your answer.
subjective.answer: Definition: The σ-algebra generated by ℬ, written σ(ℬ), is the intersection of all σ-algebras on X that contain ℬ. Since an arbitrary intersection of σ-algebras is a σ-algebra, and P(X) is one σ-algebra containing ℬ (so the family is non-empty), σ(ℬ) exists and is the smallest σ-algebra containing ℬ. For ℬ = {A}: any σ-algebra containing A must contain A′ (complementation), X = A ∪ A′ and ∅ = X′, hence must contain {∅, X, A, A′}. This collection is itself a σ-algebra: complements are ∅′ = X, X′ = ∅, (A′)′ = A, and all unions of its members stay inside it. Therefore σ({A}) = {∅, X, A, A′}.

subjective.question: Prove that for every family ℬ of subsets of X there exists a smallest σ-algebra containing ℬ.
subjective.answer: Existence: Let 䫀= { 䧀ᵢ :䧀ᵢ is a σ-algebra on X and ℬ ⊆ 䧀ᵢ, i ∈ I}. The family 䫀is non-empty because P(X) is a σ-algebra containing ℬ. Put 䨠= ∩_{i∈I} 䧀ᵢ. By the theorem on arbitrary intersections of σ-algebras, 䨠is a σ-algebra. Since ℬ ⊆ 䧀ᵢ for every i, we have ℬ ⊆ 䨠, so 䨠is a σ-algebra containing ℬ. Minimality: If 䩐is any σ-algebra containing ℬ, then 䩐∈ 䫀, so 䨠= ∩_{i∈I} 䧀ᵢ ⊆ 䩐. Hence 䨠is contained in every σ-algebra containing ℬ, i.e. 䨠is the smallest σ-algebra containing ℬ. This 䨠is the σ-algebra generated by ℬ.

subjective.question: State and prove the disjointification theorem: every sequence {Eₙ} of sets in a σ-algebra 䧀can be replaced by a pairwise disjoint sequence {Fₙ} with Fₙ ⊆ Eₙ and ∪ₙ Eₙ = ∪ₙ Fₙ.
subjective.answer: Construction: Put F₁ = E₁ and Fₙ = Eₙ − (E₁ ∪ E₂ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ₋₁) for n ≥ 2. (i) Fₙ ∈ 䧀: By De Morgan's law, Fₙ = Eₙ ∩ (E₁′ ∩ E₂′ ∩ … ∩ Eₙ₋₁′). Since Eₙ, E₁, …, Eₙ₋₁ ∈ 䧀, their complements belong to 䧀, and 䧀is closed under finite intersections, so Fₙ ∈ 䧀. (ii) Fₙ ⊆ Eₙ: Fₙ = Eₙ minus some set, so Fₙ ⊆ Eₙ. (iii) Pairwise disjoint: Let m < n. Then F_m ⊆ E_m, and Fₙ = Eₙ − (E₁ ∪ … ∪ Eₙ₋₁) excludes E_m, so F_m ∩ Fₙ ⊆ E_m ∩ Fₙ = ∅. Hence F_m ∩ Fₙ = ∅. (iv) Same union: Since Fₙ ⊆ Eₙ, ∪ₙ Fₙ ⊆ ∪ₙ Eₙ. Conversely, each x ∈ Eₙ belongs to Eₖ for a first index k ≤ n, and then x ∈ Fₖ; so ∪ₙ Eₙ ⊆ ∪ₙ Fₙ. Hence ∪ₙ Eₙ = ∪ₙ Fₙ.
